quote.translation: "Chance" comes from cadentia and hasard from casus, so that both have their source in cadere, and cadere, "to fall", has the structure of in......cadere, "to fall onto ......", as when "a stone falls onto the head of a passer-by"; like Zu-fall, it makes sense only through relativity.

regions.text: うにi...cadere（....・人落ちろ）の構造を有つたもので、Nu-Sailと同様に相對性によつて初めて意味をなすものである。

quote.translation: I have already noted that Descartes, too, uses the expression "to fall by chance into the truth" (casu incidam in veritatem) (see p. 51).

regions.text: デカルトも「偶然に眞理の中へ漱おる」（casuincidaminveritatem）いふ言ひまはしを用ひてゐることは既に云つた（五一直參照）。

quote.translation: This in-cidere, the source of the word "incident", comes, needless to say, from in-cadere.

regions.text: このin-cidereはincidentの語源であるが、云ふまでもな～in-cadereから來てゐる。

quote.translation: That an apple fell by chance into Newton's field of vision, and that, when the Eitai Bridge collapsed, Miyokichi fell by chance into the boat of Shinsuke of Chijimiya, must be said to carry a symbolic significance.

regions.text: 林檎が側然にニュ1トンの視野へ落おかことや永代橋がこはれて美代吉が側然に縮屋新助の船の中ペ落おだことは象徴約意義を有つてるると云はなければならない。またfortuitusはfortuna2同様にforsに基いてゐろものでferreから來てゐる。

quote.translation: Fortuitus, likewise, rests like fortuna on fors and comes from ferre, and this ferre, "to bring", also shows the structure of in......ferre, "to bring to ......", and so expresses relativity.

regions.text: このferre（持つて来る）るin・ferre（…・・・・へ持つて水る）の構遣を示して相對性を言ひ表はしてゐる。

quote.translation: Chance is also called tekizen (適然), and 適 is glossed as "to correspond is called 適", so that 適 clearly speaks of relativity.

regions.text: なほ偶然のことは適然とも云ばれるが「相當日適」で、適は明瞭に相對性を語つてるる。

quote.translation: Other Japanese words for chance, such as yukiatari-battari, meguriawase, shiawase and magure-atari, likewise hint at relative positive contingency.

regions.text: その他「行営りばつたり」「廻の合せ」「仕合せ」「まぐれあたり」などいふ偶然に開する語は相對積極的偶然を暗示してゐる。偶然性が甲と乙との二元の避遍に於て題著なる形態を取ることは醤宴」のプラトンも「個人の運命」のシューベンハウェルも齊しく認酸したことである。

quote.translation: That contingency takes a marked form in the Encounter of two elements, A and B, was recognised alike by Plato in the Symposium and by Schopenhauer in "The Fate of the Individual".

Consider the legend in the Kojiki in which the two gods Izanagi and Izanami, saying "You go round from the right and meet me, I will go round from the left and meet you", "went round the heavenly pillar and met".
